title: Creature Clash: Duel Loop Prototype
transcript: So, uh, Poké Clash or Creature Clash is a mobile creature battling game built around the fantasy of becoming the greatest trainer alive. You start with a single companion creature and set out on a journey, walking routes, catching wild creatures to grow your collection, and battling other trainers along the way. Every battle is a duel of stats. Each creature is scored against a handful of categories like attack, attack, defense, speed, and special powers. And in battle, you pick which category to fight on turn by whittling down your opponent's health. On top of the raw numbers sit 2 layers of depth. First, elemental types— fire, water, grass, electric, and rock— that beat the— that beat and lose to each other in a rock-paper-scissors triangle. So your strongest strat can be neutralized by a bad matchup, and category choice becomes a real read against your opponent. Second unique abilities each creature carries bend the rules of the duel: stealing a strat, forcing a category, shrugging off a type disadvantage. This is of course V3. The world is structured as a series of gems— gyms, G-Y-M-S, gyms. Each themed around a type and guarded by a leader. Beat the leader, earn a badge, and after a hard-won victory of a 3v3 duel, you even get to swap one of your creatures for one of theirs. Collect all the badges, top the leaderboard, and prove you're the best. The long-term vision is online multiplayer where trainers battle each other directly, but the heart of it is a single-player story mode you can lose yourself in. In the initial phase of project, the multi— we would go with the single-player story mode where the other trainers would be AI-powered. This is a passion project first, an idea that's been kicking around for years, and this is about finally building it as interactive and as fun as it can possibly be. On strategy, the plan is to prototype privately against real creature data to nail down whether the loop is generally fun, even without worrying about art or originality. And only later, if the game proves worth it, invest in a set of original creatures. For anything that goes public, validate the fun first, own the world second. Another feature that we should be adding in this would be XP and progression. With each battle, with each duel of a creature, with each winning, losing, or drawing, of a creature, the creature would be earning XP, experience points, and those experience points would then be used by their trainer to increase their categories. Any of the categories could be used by that. So yeah, that's all.

prd.oneLiner: A private single-player prototype testing whether a classic stat-category duel, type triangle, and rule-bending abilities can out-strategize the card-based and gesture-based combat that current mobile creature collectors ship with.
prd.problem: Trainers who grew up on Pokémon-style games want the fantasy of raising a creature, out-thinking a rival, and proving mastery through direct head-to-head duels — but today they either play nostalgia-driven originals or settle for mobile alternatives that reframe combat as card-hand play (Creature Clash: Echoes) or gesture-drawing minigames (Poke Clash), diluting the read-your-opponent tension of picking a stat category under a type disadvantage. The founder has held this idea for years and currently has no way to test it beyond imagination; there is no build yet, private or public, and no evidence the stat-duel-plus-abilities loop is actually fun before investing in original art or a live release. Existing competitors also lack a persistent gym/badge journey or a post-battle creature swap, meaning even players drawn to the genre have no mobile product offering structured trainer-vs-leader progression with tangible stakes for winning.
prd.targetUser: The founder themself, acting as the sole private playtester of a personal passion project, prototyping to determine if the core battle loop is fun before showing it to anyone else.

must_have.title: Starter creature & wild catching
must_have.rationale: Named as the opening hook of the journey in the transcript and is table-stakes for the genre per competitor analysis.
must_have.description: Player begins with a single companion creature and can catch additional wild creatures encountered while walking routes.

must_have.title: Stat-category duel system
must_have.rationale: This is the heart of the idea as described by the founder and the product's core differentiator from competitors' card- and gesture-based combat.
must_have.description: Battles are turn-based duels where each side picks a category (attack, defense, speed, special) to fight on, whittling down opponent HP.

must_have.title: Elemental type triangle
must_have.rationale: Explicitly specified by the founder as the first depth layer on top of raw stats, and type triangles are table stakes across all competitors.
must_have.description: Five types — fire, water, grass, electric, rock — beat and lose to each other in a rock-paper-scissors pattern that modifies duel outcomes.

must_have.title: Unique creature abilities
must_have.rationale: Founder describes this as the second core depth layer; research flags it as a whitespace deeper than competitors' Marks/Momentum systems.
must_have.description: Each creature carries an ability that bends duel rules — stealing a strat, forcing a category, or negating a type disadvantage.

must_have.title: Gym/badge structure with leaders
must_have.rationale: Directly specified in the transcript as the world's structure and identified as a differentiation opportunity neither competitor offers.
must_have.description: World is organized into gyms, each themed around a type and guarded by a leader; beating a leader awards a badge.

must_have.title: Post-gym 3v3 creature swap
must_have.rationale: Explicitly described by the founder as a reward mechanic and confirmed by research as a gap no competitor addresses.
must_have.description: After winning a 3v3 duel against a gym leader, the player swaps one of their creatures for one of the leader's.

must_have.title: XP and trainer-directed stat growth
must_have.rationale: Founder explicitly calls this out as a feature to add, and research flags player-directed stat allocation as a gap versus competitors' automatic evolution stages.
must_have.description: Creatures earn XP from every battle outcome (win, lose, or draw), which the trainer allocates across any stat category.

must_have.title: AI-powered single-player trainers
must_have.rationale: Transcript explicitly scopes phase one to single-player story mode with AI trainers, deferring multiplayer.
must_have.description: In this initial phase, all opposing trainers encountered on routes and in gyms are AI-controlled rather than live players.

must_have.title: Prototype on real creature data, no original art
must_have.rationale: Founder's stated strategy: validate the fun of the loop privately before investing in original creatures or art.
must_have.description: Build and balance the loop using existing/placeholder creature data and stats rather than original designs.

should_have.title: Persistent open-world route exploration
should_have.rationale: Creature Clash: Echoes resets progress via procedurally generated roguelite runs on defeat; a persistent journey better matches the founder's route-walking framing and is a stated differentiation opportunity.
should_have.description: Routes and gyms form a continuous walkable world state that persists between sessions, rather than resetting.

should_have.title: Badge-linked trainer leaderboard
should_have.rationale: Poke Clash offers only a simple friend-ranking leaderboard; tying ranking to badge/gym progression better reflects the founder's 'top the leaderboard, prove you're the best' framing.
should_have.description: Leaderboard ranks the player against tracked AI trainers by badges earned, not just battles won.

could_have.title: Online trainer-vs-trainer multiplayer
could_have.rationale: Founder names this as the long-term vision but explicitly defers it past the initial phase; research confirms neither competitor offers stated PvP.
could_have.description: Direct PvP battles between real trainers using the same stat-duel, type, and ability system.

could_have.title: Original creature roster & artwork
could_have.rationale: Founder's own stated sequencing: invest in original creatures only after the loop proves fun, so it belongs later than V1.
could_have.description: Replace placeholder/real creature data with an original, owned set of creature designs and art.

could_have.title: Expanded ability library
could_have.rationale: Research identifies the ability layer as deeper than competitors' systems and worth expanding once core viability is proven.
could_have.description: Grow the pool of unique, rule-bending abilities beyond the initial launch set once the base loop is validated.

wont_have.title: Monetization / in-app purchases
wont_have.rationale: This is a private prototype validating fun first, not a public release, so monetization is out of scope per the founder's stated strategy.
wont_have.description: No energy systems, currency packs, or subscription passes in this version.

wont_have.title: Creature trading between players
wont_have.rationale: Offered by Creature Clash: Echoes but not mentioned by the founder and irrelevant to a single-player private prototype.
wont_have.description: No mechanism to trade creatures with other trainers.

wont_have.title: Egg hatching acquisition ritual
wont_have.rationale: The founder specifies catching wild creatures on routes as the acquisition method, not hatching, explicitly diverging from both competitors' egg systems.

wont_have.title: Procedurally generated roguelite run structure
wont_have.rationale: Competitor Creature Clash: Echoes uses this structure; the founder's route-walking, persistent-world framing explicitly rejects it.
wont_have.description: No procedurally generated maps or run-based resets on defeat.

wont_have.title: Card-based or gesture-drawing combat
wont_have.rationale: Both competitors use these mechanics; the founder's stat-category duel system is the explicit alternative being tested.
wont_have.description: No card-hand mechanics or gesture/shape-drawing inputs for battling.

wont_have.title: Public app store release & account system
wont_have.rationale: Transcript frames this explicitly as a private prototype to validate fun before any public investment.
wont_have.description: No App Store/Google Play publishing, sign-in, or cloud save/backup in this phase.

wont_have.title: Daily arenas, equippable relics, and cosmetic variants
wont_have.rationale: These are extra systems from Creature Clash: Echoes that add scope without testing the core duel loop the founder wants validated first.
wont_have.description: No Proving-Grounds-style daily challenge modes, equippable relic items, or shiny/rare cosmetic creature variants.

nonGoals: Not building or publishing to app stores in this phase — remains a private prototype.
Not implementing online multiplayer or live PvP battling in V1.
Not designing or commissioning original creature art or IP for this phase.
Not building any monetization, account, or cloud-sync systems.
Not supporting more than the five specified elemental types at launch.
risks: The stat-duel-plus-abilities loop may not prove meaningfully more fun than card- or gesture-based alternatives once actually played, invalidating the core bet.
Balancing five types plus per-creature unique abilities and trainer-directed XP allocation could produce dominant strategies that flatten the intended 'read your opponent' tension.
Using real/existing creature data during prototyping carries IP risk if the build is ever shown publicly or shared before original creatures are developed.
As a solo passion project, the combined scope of gyms, swap mechanics, abilities, and XP allocation risks stalling before the core loop is even validated.
openQuestions: How many gyms/badges constitute a complete V1 story mode for playtesting purposes?
What threshold of fun/completion data triggers the decision to invest in original creature art?
Should XP-driven stat allocation be fully player-controlled per category, or guided with suggested distributions?
Which existing creature dataset will be used for prototyping, and what are the legal constraints on using it even privately?

competitiveLandscape.positioningDelta: Replaces its card-hand/Momentum roguelite combat and procedurally reset runs with a persistent stat-category duel, type triangle, and rule-bending abilities inside a continuous gym/badge world.
Replaces its gesture-drawing capture/combat mechanic with strategic, stat-based turn-by-turn dueling and a structured gym/leader progression it lacks.

research.marketSummary: The competitive set is small but directly adjacent to the proposed idea: mobile creature-collector games that borrow heavily from the Pokémon formula (hatching, evolving, elemental type advantages, and a trainer journey). Creature Clash: Echoes is the closest analog, already live on iOS and Android as a free-to-play card-based roguelite with a 4-element triangle, evolution, and light narrative, though it reports very low download numbers on Google Play. Poke Clash is an older (2018-era) mobile title using gesture-drawing combat rather than stat-based dueling, with a simpler catch-and-train loop. Neither competitor is stated to offer a persistent open-world gym/badge structure, direct trainer-vs-trainer swapping of creatures, or player-vs-player online multiplayer, leaving room for differentiation in structured progression and social battling.
research.ourPositioning: Where existing mobile creature collectors lean on card-based roguelite combat (Creature Clash: Echoes) or gesture-drawing capture mechanics (Poke Clash), this product differentiates with a classic stat-duel battle system layered with type match-ups and rule-bending unique abilities, wrapped in a persistent gym-and-badge journey with trainer-vs-leader creature swaps and, eventually, direct online PvP — validating the core duel loop first before investing in original creature art.

engineering.overview: A private, single-player web prototype for validating a stat-category duel loop before any art or public release is built. There are no other players, no accounts, and no cloud sync in scope, so the architecture is deliberately local-first: a Next.js client running entirely in the founder's browser, with all creature, battle, and playtest data stored in an on-device SQLite database. Nothing about the duel, the world, or the AI trainers depends on a server, so no backend API is built. The one thing this project must get right is the turn-resolution logic for the stat duel (type triangle + abilities + growth), so that component is designed first and in depth; everything else (world navigation, roster growth, gym/badge progression, AI opponents, telemetry) is built around feeding it clean inputs and recording its outputs for balance analysis.
engineering.dataFlow: On launch, the Next.js client loads the Creature & Content Data Layer and the founder's save file from local SQLite. The player navigates the route/gym map (World Route Navigation); encountering a wild creature or trainer starts a Battle row. Each round, the player picks a category in the UI while the AI Trainer Decision Engine picks for the opponent; both choices go into the Duel Battle Engine, which applies the type chart and any ability effects, resolves HP deltas, and appends a BattleTurn row. When a battle ends, Creature Roster & Growth awards XP and prompts stat allocation (written as an idempotent XPAllocation); if it was a deciding gym battle, Gym & Badge Progression issues a Badge and runs the idempotent GymSwap. All writes land in the local SQLite database — nothing is sent to a server. Playtest Telemetry logs the session and the founder periodically exports the SQLite file/JSON to review against the success metrics.

components.name: Duel Battle Engine
components.responsibility: The core of the product. Inputs per round: the two active creatures (stats after growth allocation, current HP, ability, elemental type), the category each side picks that round (attack/defense/speed/special), and a seeded RNG value for the battle. Outputs: which side wins the round, the HP delta applied, whether an ability fired and what it changed, and an immutable BattleTurn log row. Category choices are revealed simultaneously, the type-triangle multiplier is applied, abilities resolve in a fixed documented order (steal > force > negate-disadvantage > other), and the same battle_id, rng_seed and choice sequence always reproduce the same outcome, so balance bugs are reproducible.

components.name: Ability Rules Registry
components.responsibility: Defines the launch set of unique creature abilities as structured trigger/effect data (steal-category, force-category, negate-type-disadvantage, etc.) that the Battle Engine reads and resolves; keeps rule-bending logic declarative and testable rather than hard-coded per creature.

components.name: AI Trainer Decision Engine
components.responsibility: Deterministic, rule-based (non-LLM) heuristics that choose a category for every AI-controlled opponent — wild creatures, route trainers, and gym leaders — e.g. counter the player's last category, lean into a type advantage, or protect a low-HP creature. Kept deterministic so duel outcomes stay reproducible for balance testing.

components.name: Creature Roster & Growth
components.responsibility: Tracks each owned CreatureInstance's stats, HP, and ability; awards XP after every battle (win, lose, or draw) and exposes the trainer-directed allocation UI that lets the player assign earned XP to any stat category, writing an idempotent XPAllocation record per battle per creature.

components.name: Gym & Badge Progression
components.responsibility: Models the ordered sequence of gyms, each with a type theme and a leader trainer; issues a Badge on a 3v3 gym win and runs the post-gym creature swap (player gives one creature, receives one of the leader's), recorded as a single idempotent GymSwap transaction keyed to the deciding battle.

components.name: World Route Navigation & Wild Catching
components.responsibility: Renders the persistent, walkable route/gym map, resolves wild encounters from each route's weighted species table, and handles the starter-selection and catch flow that adds a new CreatureInstance to the roster.

components.name: Creature & Content Data Layer
components.responsibility: Loads and serves the placeholder/real creature species, base stats, types, and ability definitions used for prototyping (per the founder's stated strategy of validating the loop before original art); isolated behind one module so the real dataset can later be swapped for original creatures without touching the Battle Engine.

components.name: Local Persistence & Save Layer
components.responsibility: Owns the on-device SQLite database (schema below): reads/writes all game state, exposes save export/import as a file so the founder can back up a playtest run manually, since no cloud sync is in scope.

components.name: Playtest Telemetry & Leaderboard
components.responsibility: Logs PlaytestSession records (duration, self-reported 1–5 fun score, battles played) and derives the four success metrics (completion rate, session frequency, fun score, category variety) plus a simple badge-count leaderboard against the tracked AI trainers, all computed locally from the SQLite tables.

techStack.llm: Not required. AI trainers use deterministic, rule-based heuristics (e.g. counter the player's last category, lean into a type advantage, protect low-HP creatures) rather than a generative model, so battle outcomes stay reproducible for the seeded-RNG replay requirement and the 'category-choice variety' success metric. All stat math, type-triangle multipliers, XP, and swap logic are deterministic code, never model output.
techStack.auth: Not required. Single local player, no account system per PRD non-goals; the app opens straight into the on-device save file.
techStack.infra: No cloud infra required to run the prototype; launched via local dev/build on the founder's machine. Optional unlisted Vercel static deploy only to test on a phone browser — it would serve JS/asset bundles only, never game data, keeping the 'no public release' non-goal intact.
techStack.backend: No server/API layer. All game, duel, and progression logic runs client-side in the browser — this is a single local player with no accounts or multiplayer, so a backend would add infrastructure the PRD explicitly excludes.
techStack.database: Client-side SQLite via sql.js (WASM), persisted to the browser's OPFS/IndexedDB on the founder's own device. No cloud database, so no game or playtest data is ever transmitted anywhere — matches the PRD's explicit 'no cloud sync' non-goal.
techStack.devtools: TypeScript, ESLint/Prettier as standard; Vitest unit tests specifically around the Duel Battle Engine's round-resolution function, since its correctness and determinism are what the whole validation effort depends on.
techStack.frontend: Next.js (App Router) as a local-first single-page client; no SSR or multi-tenant needs for a solo private prototype.

tasks.title: Local schema & persistence setup
tasks.description: Stand up the sql.js (SQLite/WASM) database from the schema above inside the browser, with OPFS/IndexedDB-backed storage, a migration runner, and a manual save-file export/import so a multi-week playtest isn't lost to browser storage eviction.

tasks.title: Access setup (no-op, single local profile)
tasks.description: Confirm the app boots directly into one local save with no login screen, and add a guard/lint rule preventing any accidental network or cloud-service calls from creeping into the client, per the no-accounts/no-cloud-sync non-goals.

tasks.title: Local run & deploy setup
tasks.description: Configure `next dev`/local static build as the primary way to run the prototype; wire an optional unlisted Vercel deploy for phone-browser testing that ships client assets only, with no data endpoints.

tasks.title: Duel Battle Engine core
tasks.description: Implement the deterministic round-resolution algorithm: category reveal, type-triangle multiplier lookup, fixed-order ability resolution, stat comparison, HP delta, and BattleTurn logging, backed by a seeded RNG and a full Vitest suite covering type/ability edge cases.

tasks.title: Ability Rules Registry & launch ability set
tasks.description: Build the trigger/effect data model for abilities (steal-category, force-category, negate-type-disadvantage) and author the initial roster's abilities against it, decoupled from the Battle Engine's core loop.

tasks.title: AI Trainer Decision Engine
tasks.description: Implement rule-based category-selection heuristics for wild encounters, route trainers, and gym leaders, with distinct difficulty/decision profiles per Trainer.decisionProfile.

tasks.title: Creature Roster & XP Growth flow
tasks.description: Build the XP-earning logic for every battle outcome (win/lose/draw) and the trainer-directed stat-allocation UI, writing one idempotent XPAllocation row per battle per creature.

tasks.title: Gym/Badge progression & 3v3 swap
tasks.description: Implement gym sequencing, badge issuance on a 3v3 gym win, and the post-gym creature swap as a single idempotent GymSwap transaction keyed to the deciding battle.

tasks.title: World route navigation & wild catching
tasks.description: Build the persistent route/gym map, weighted wild-encounter resolution from RouteEncounter data, starter selection, and the catch flow that creates a new CreatureInstance.

tasks.title: Playtest telemetry & metrics export
tasks.description: Log PlaytestSession records (duration, 1-5 fun score, battles played) and add an export view that computes the four PRD success metrics directly from the local SQLite tables.
